summary: This document describes Pandoc2rfc, a technique for writing Internet-Drafts and RFCs in a Markdown variant called Pandoc plus a small amount of XML. The aim is to let authors focus on the text without heavy XML tagging, though some typesetting knowledge is still needed.

eli5.summary: Writing a document with lots of special codes is tiring. This RFC shows a way to write in simple everyday text with just a few codes, then turn it into a proper RFC.

questions: how to author an internet-draft with pandoc
subtitle: Authoring RFCs and Internet-Drafts in Markdown instead of XML.

tldr.problem: Writing Internet-Drafts and RFCs in XML is tedious and distracting; authors must deal with heavy XML markup while focusing on content.
tldr.mechanism: Pandoc2rfc is a technique that lets authors write in Pandoc (a Markdown variant), then automatically converts it to DocBook XML and finally to RFC format using standard tools.
tldr.outcome: Authors can focus on writing text with minimal markup, though they still need to edit some XML for metadata and references. The tool chain works but adds a transformation step.

today: RFC 7328 is an Informational RFC published in August 2014. Pandoc2rfc remains a viable tool for authors who prefer Markdown but must deliver RFCs in XML. It is used by some RFC authors, though many continue to write directly in XML.

sections.title: The Problem and Solution
sections.content:
RFC 7328 introduces Pandoc2rfc, a technique for writing Internet-Drafts (I-Ds) and RFCs using Pandoc, a Markdown syntax variant, combined with a small amount of XML as defined in RFC 2629.

The core goal is to let authors focus on the main body of text without being distracted by XML tags. However, the RFC is honest: Pandoc2rfc does not eliminate the need to edit XML files entirely. Specifically, the "front" section of an RFC (which contains metadata like authors, dates, and references) still requires XML editing.

Pandoc is particularly well-suited for RFC-like documents because it is almost plain text and can be translated to numerous output formats including HTML, EPUB, Markdown, and DocBook XML.
sections.eli5: You write your main text in simple Markdown. A tool converts it to proper XML. But you still need to edit the title page and reference list in XML.

sections.title: The Conversion Pipeline
sections.content:
Pandoc2rfc works in three steps. First, Pandoc converts Markdown source files to DocBook XML, which is a structured XML format for technical documents. Second, an XSLT stylesheet (specifically transform.xsl) processes the DocBook XML and produces output suitable for the "middle" or "back" section of an RFC.

Third, the xml2rfc tool (the standard RFC formatting tool) takes the final XML template and produces text or HTML output.

The setup requires editing four files: an abstract.mkd file, a middle.mkd file containing the main body, a back.mkd file for appendices, and a template.xml file that holds author and reference information. The conversion can be done with simple shell commands combining pandoc, xsltproc, and xml2rfc.
sections.eli5: Markdown becomes DocBook, which becomes RFC XML, which becomes the final document. Each step is a simple transformation.

sections.title: What Pandoc2rfc Supports
sections.content:
Pandoc2rfc supports many RFC authoring features. Sections can have anchors and titles. Lists are supported in multiple styles: bullet points, numbered lists, lettered lists (both uppercase and lowercase), and Roman numerals (both uppercase and lowercase). Definition lists using Pandoc syntax are also supported.

Text formatting includes verbatim code (using backticks), emphasis (underscores), and strong emphasis (double asterisks). Figures and tables can be created with Pandoc syntax and assigned titles and anchors. References work both as external links and cross-references to sections, figures, and tables. Processing instructions (special directives appearing as <?rfc?>) are carried through to the generated XML, and the <vspace> tag for vertical spacing is supported.

An index can be generated using Pandoc footnote syntax. The specification includes a cheat sheet table showing all these constructs and their Pandoc syntax.
sections.eli5: You can write bold, code, lists, tables, figures, and references in Markdown. The tool understands all of these.

sections.title: Limitations and Unsupported Features
sections.content:
Despite its benefits, Pandoc2rfc has important limitations. The initial setup requires editing XML files for the template and reference library. Pandoc's "Title Block" metadata feature is not used; authors must put metadata (title, authors, dates, keywords, and URLs) directly into template.xml.

Citations use cross-reference syntax rather than Pandoc's native citation syntax. Comments must be written as HTML comments in the Pandoc source files. Most importantly, authors still need to understand and deal with possible errors from xml2rfc, which can be cryptic.

Some RFC constructs that require complex formatting still cannot be expressed purely in Pandoc and demand direct XML editing. The tool is a convenience layer rather than a complete solution to the XML complexity problem.
sections.eli5: You still need to learn some XML for the title page and references. If something goes wrong, you may need to debug XML files.

sections.title: Building an Internet-Draft
sections.content:
The basic workflow is straightforward. Create three Markdown files: abstract.mkd, middle.mkd, and back.mkd. For each, run pandoc -st docbook FILENAME.mkd | xsltproc --nonet transform.xsl - > FILENAME.xml to produce the XML. Create a template.xml file with the front matter (using RFC 2629 XML syntax).

Once the XML files are ready, use xml2rfc to generate output: xml2rfc template.xml -f draft.txt --text creates text output, xml2rfc template.xml -f draft.html --html creates HTML, and xml2rfc template.xml -f draft.xml --exp creates XML. The Pandoc2rfc source repository includes a shell script that automates these steps, so authors can simply run pandoc2rfc *.mkd.

Dependencies include Pandoc, xsltproc (the XSLT processor), and xml2rfc version 2 or higher. The tool has been used successfully by RFC authors since its introduction.
sections.eli5: Write your three Markdown files, run some commands to convert them, then use xml2rfc to make the final document. The process is automated by a shell script.
